title: Indefinite Articles: ein / eine
simpleExplanation: 'ein' and 'eine' mean 'a/an'. ein goes with masculine and neuter nouns; eine with feminine nouns.
detailedExplanation: German has no separate word for 'a' — you use ein/eine based on the noun's gender. ein (der/ein Mann), ein (das/ein Buch), eine (die/eine Frau). The negative is kein/keine ('not a'). Remember the gender of the noun decides the article.
usage: ein Mann | ein Buch | eine Frau | kein Geld
avoidWhen: Don't use 'einen' in the nominative — that's the accusative form. The plural has no indefinite article (Männer, not eine Männer).
simpleExplanation_en: 'ein' and 'eine' mean 'a/an'. ein goes with masculine and neuter nouns; eine with feminine nouns.
simpleExplanation_id: 'ein' dan 'eine' berarti 'sebuah'. ein untuk kata benda maskulin dan netral; eine untuk feminin.
detailedExplanation_en: German has no separate word for 'a' — you use ein/eine based on the noun's gender. ein (der/ein Mann), ein (das/ein Buch), eine (die/eine Frau). The negative is kein/keine ('not a'). Remember the gender of the noun decides the article.
detailedExplanation_id: Bahasa Jerman tidak punya kata khusus untuk 'sebuah' — pakai ein/eine sesuai gender kata benda. ein (der/ein Mann), ein (das/ein Buch), eine (die/eine Frau). Bentuk negatifnya kein/keine ('bukan sebuah'). Ingat gender kata benda menentukan artikelnya.
usage_en: ein Mann | ein Buch | eine Frau | kein Geld
usage_id: ein Mann | ein Buch | eine Frau | kein Geld

title: Formal vs Informal Address (Sie vs du)
simpleExplanation: German has two ways to say 'you': 'Sie' for formal situations and 'du' for informal.
detailedExplanation: Use 'Sie' with strangers, in professional settings, with elders, or anyone you address by last name. Use 'du' with friends, family, children, and people who've invited you to use it. 'Sie' is always capitalized and uses third-person plural verb forms.
usage: Sie: Wie heißen Sie? (formal) | du: Wie heißt du? (informal)
avoidWhen: Don't use 'du' with strangers or in professional contexts unless invited.

examples.translation: Good day, what is your name? (formal)
examples.translation_en: Good day, what is your name? (formal)

commonMistakes: Using 'du' with strangers or in formal settings
Using wrong verb conjugation with Sie

title: Grammatical Gender and Articles
simpleExplanation: All German nouns have a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das).
detailedExplanation: Every German noun belongs to one of three genders, which affects the article and adjective endings. The gender often doesn't correspond to biological sex or English patterns. Must be memorized with each noun. Plural always uses 'die'.
usage: Learn gender with every noun: der Mann, die Frau, das Kind.
avoidWhen: Don't assume gender based on English or biological sex.

examples.text: der Tisch (m), die Tür (f), das Fenster (n)
examples.translation: the table, the door, the window
examples.translation_en: the table, the door, the window

examples.text: die Tische, die Türen, die Fenster (plural)
examples.translation: the tables, the doors, the windows
examples.translation_en: the tables, the doors, the windows

title: Imperative (Giving Commands)
pattern: du: lern-e! | Sie: lernen Sie! | wir: lernen wir!
simpleExplanation: Use the imperative to give orders or requests. There are forms for du, Sie, and wir.
detailedExplanation: du-form: drop the -st ending (du lernst → Lern!), add -e for stems in -t/-d/-m/-n (Arbeite!). Sie-form: infinitive + Sie (Lernen Sie!). wir-form: infinitive + wir (Gehen wir!). Informal you can add 'mal' to soften: Komm mal her! The verb comes first.
usage: Lern Deutsch! | Arbeiten Sie! | Gehen wir!
avoidWhen: Don't use the du-form to address strangers — use the polite Sie-form instead.
commonMistakes: Using du-imperative with strangers (should be Sie)
Putting the verb in second position instead of first

title: Modal Verbs (können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, mögen)
simpleExplanation: Modal verbs express ability (können), necessity (müssen), desire (wollen), permission (dürfen), obligation (sollen), or liking (mögen).
detailedExplanation: Modal verbs are irregular and conjugated in second position. The main verb stays in infinitive form at the end of the clause. Common modals: können (can), müssen (must), wollen (want to), dürfen (may), sollen (should), mögen (like to). They have stem changes in singular.
usage: Ich kann schwimmen. (I can swim.) | Du musst lernen. (You must learn.)
avoidWhen: Don't put main verb in second position with modals.

examples.translation: We want to go to the cinema.
examples.translation_en: We want to go to the cinema.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the main verb instead of modal

title: Negation with 'nicht' and 'kein'
simpleExplanation: Use 'kein' to negate nouns (no/not a), and 'nicht' to negate everything else.
detailedExplanation: 'kein' replaces the indefinite article (ein) and means 'no/not a/not any'. It declines like 'ein'. 'nicht' negates verbs, adjectives, and entire sentences. Position: 'nicht' comes before what it negates, usually before predicate adjectives/nouns or at end of sentence.
usage: Ich habe kein Auto. (no car) | Das ist nicht gut. (not good)
avoidWhen: Don't use 'nicht ein' for nouns - use 'kein'.

examples.text: Das ist nicht mein Buch. (not mine)

title: Plural Forms of Nouns
simpleExplanation: German plurals are formed in several ways: -e, -en, -er, -n, -s, or no change, sometimes with an umlaut.
detailedExplanation: Most masculine/feminine nouns take -e/-en; many neuter nouns take -er or stay the same; foreign words take -s; nouns ending in -e take -n. Many vowels get an umlaut in the plural: der Mann → die Männer, die Mutter → die Mütter. You must learn the plural together with the noun.
avoidWhen: Don't add -s to German native nouns (that's only for foreign/loan words).
commonMistakes: Guessing the plural instead of learning it

title: Possessive Pronouns
pattern: mein (my), dein (your), sein/ihr/sein (his/her/its), unser (our), euer (your pl), ihr/Ihr (their/your formal)
simpleExplanation: Possessive pronouns show ownership and must agree with the gender of the noun they modify.
detailedExplanation: Possessive pronouns take endings like indefinite articles: mein/meine/mein (m/f/n). They agree with the possessed noun's gender, not the possessor's. Endings change based on case (nominative: mein/meine/mein, accusative: meinen/meine/mein).
usage: mein Vater (m), meine Mutter (f), mein Kind (n)
avoidWhen: Don't forget to match the possessed noun's gender.

examples.text: Das ist mein Bruder und meine Schwester.
examples.translation: That is my brother and my sister.
examples.translation_en: That is my brother and my sister.
examples.translation_id: Itu saudara laki-laki dan saudara perempuan saya.

title: Present Tense (Präsens)
pattern: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en
simpleExplanation: German present tense conjugates verbs with endings that match the subject pronoun.
detailedExplanation: Regular verbs add endings to the stem: -e (ich), -st (du), -t (er/sie/es), -en (wir/sie/Sie), -t (ihr). Stem-changing verbs modify vowel in du/er forms (e→i: geben→gibst, e→ie: sehen→siehst, a→ä: fahren→fährst).
usage: ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen, ihr lernt, sie lernen
avoidWhen: Don't forget stem changes in irregular verbs.

examples.text: Ich lerne Deutsch. Du lernst auch.
examples.translation: I learn German. You learn too.
examples.translation_en: I learn German. You learn too.
examples.translation_id: Saya belajar bahasa Jerman. Kamu juga belajar.

simpleExplanation_en: German present tense conjugates verbs with endings that match the subject pronoun.

title: Personal Pronouns
pattern: ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie
simpleExplanation: German personal pronouns: ich (I), du (you informal), er/sie/es (he/she/it), wir (we), ihr (you plural), sie (they), Sie (you formal).
detailedExplanation: German has distinct pronouns for all persons. Third person has three genders: er (masculine), sie (feminine), es (neuter). The formal 'Sie' is capitalized and uses same form as 'sie' (they) but with capital S.
usage: Use pronouns according to person, number, and formality.
avoidWhen: Don't confuse sie (she/they) with Sie (you formal).

examples.text: Ich bin Student. Du bist Lehrerin.
examples.translation: I am a student. You are a teacher.
examples.translation_en: I am a student. You are a teacher.
examples.translation_id: Saya adalah pelajar. Kamu adalah guru.

examples.text: Er ist groß. Sie ist klein.
examples.translation: He is tall. She is small.
examples.translation_en: He is tall. She is small.

simpleExplanation_en: German personal pronouns: ich (I), du (you informal), er/sie/es (he/she/it), wir (we), ihr (you plural), sie (they), Sie (you formal).
simpleExplanation_id: Kata ganti orang Jerman: ich (saya), du (kamu informal), er/sie/es (dia), wir (kami), ihr (kalian), sie (mereka), Sie (Anda formal).
detailedExplanation_en: German has distinct pronouns for all persons. Third person has three genders: er (masculine), sie (feminine), es (neuter). The formal 'Sie' is capitalized and uses same form as 'sie' (they) but with capital S.
detailedExplanation_id: Bahasa Jerman punya kata ganti berbeda untuk semua orang. Orang ketiga punya tiga gender: er (maskulin), sie (feminin), es (netral). 'Sie' formal kapital dan memakai bentuk yang sama dengan 'sie' (mereka) tapi S besar.

title: Asking Questions (W-Fragen & Ja/Nein-Fragen)
simpleExplanation: German has two question types: W-questions (with question words) and yes/no questions (verb first).
detailedExplanation: W-questions use question words (wer, was, wo, wann, wie, warum, etc.) in first position, then verb, then subject. Yes/no questions start with verb, then subject. Both invert subject and verb from normal word order.
usage: Wer bist du? (Who are you?) | Bist du Student? (Are you a student?)
avoidWhen: Don't forget verb-subject inversion in questions.
simpleExplanation_en: German has two question types: W-questions (with question words) and yes/no questions (verb first).
simpleExplanation_id: Bahasa Jerman punya dua jenis pertanyaan: W-pertanyaan (dengan kata tanya) dan ya/tidak (kata kerja di depan).
detailedExplanation_en: W-questions use question words (wer, was, wo, wann, wie, warum, etc.) in first position, then verb, then subject. Yes/no questions start with verb, then subject. Both invert subject and verb from normal word order.

title: Separable Verbs
simpleExplanation: Some German verbs have separable prefixes that split off and move to the end of the sentence.
detailedExplanation: Separable verbs consist of a verb stem and a stressed prefix (auf-, an-, ein-, aus-, mit-, etc.). In present tense main clauses, the prefix separates and moves to sentence end. In subordinate clauses and with modal verbs, it stays attached. Common separable verbs: aufstehen (get up), anfangen (begin), einladen (invite).
usage: aufstehen: Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf. (I get up at 7 o'clock.)
avoidWhen: In subordinate clauses, the prefix stays attached.

examples.text: Ich stehe jeden Tag um 7 Uhr auf.
examples.translation: I get up every day at 7 o'clock.
examples.translation_en: I get up every day at 7 o'clock.
examples.translation_id: Saya bangun setiap hari jam tujuh.

title: Verb Conjugation (Regular Verbs)
pattern: ich lern-e, du lern-st, er/sie/es lern-t ...
simpleExplanation: Regular German verbs change their ending depending on who is doing the action.
detailedExplanation: Take the stem (verb minus -en/-n) and add: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. Examples with 'lernen': ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen, ihr lernt, sie lernen. Stems ending in -t/-d/-m/-n (like 'arbeiten') add an extra -e: du arbeitest, er arbeitet.
usage: ich lerne | du lernst | er/sie/es lernt | wir lernen | ihr lernt | sie/Sie lernen
avoidWhen: Don't forget the -e after stems ending in -t or -d (arbeiten → du arbeitest, not du arbeitst).
commonMistakes: Using the infinitive in main clauses
simpleExplanation_en: Regular German verbs change their ending depending on who is doing the action.
simpleExplanation_id: Kata kerja Jerman beraturan mengubah akhiran sesuai subjek yang melakukan aksi.
detailedExplanation_en: Take the stem (verb minus -en/-n) and add: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. Examples with 'lernen': ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen, ihr lernt, sie lernen. Stems ending in -t/-d/-m/-n (like 'arbeiten') add an extra -e: du arbeitest, er arbeitet.
detailedExplanation_id: Ambil akar kata kerja (kata kerja tanpa -en/-n) lalu tambahkan: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. title: Basic Word Order (SVO)
simpleExplanation: In German main clauses, the verb is always in the second position.
detailedExplanation: German uses V2 word order: the conjugated verb must be in second position. The first position can be subject, time expression, or other element. When first position is not subject, subject moves after verb (inversion). Subordinate clauses move verb to end.
usage: Position 1 + Verb + Subject + ... | Zeit + Verb + Subject + ...
avoidWhen: Don't put verb in first or third position in main clauses.

examples.text: Heute trinke ich Wasser. (Time first, subject after verb)

title: Word Order: Inversion
simpleExplanation: When a sentence starts with something other than the subject, the verb stays in position 2 and the subject moves behind it.
detailedExplanation: German verbs must stay in position 2. Normally the subject is first: Ich bin gestern im Kino. If you move a time word first, the subject jumps after the verb: Gestern bin ich im Kino. This inversion is very common and sounds natural in German.
usage: Ich bin gestern im Kino. → Gestern bin ich im Kino.
avoidWhen: Don't put the verb after the time word (Gestern ich bin ... is wrong).

examples.translation: Yesterday I was at the cinema.
